Modern.tagline: The return is the second storefront.
Modern.brandDescription: Backhaul is a returns-as-a-service platform built on one refusal: the refund is the last resort, not the default. Every flow it ships is exchange-first, credit-second, refund-third, and every dashboard leads with saved revenue rather than processed volume. Brands plug Backhaul into their storefront and their reverse logistics in a week, then watch the return become a second conversion event.
Modern.scope: A returns portal, exchange engine, and reverse-logistics orchestration layer for DTC brands doing 10k-500k orders a year. Includes carrier label generation, box-free drop-off partnerships, and a disposition rules engine deciding restock, refurbish, donate, or destroy per item.
Modern.brandNameRationale: Backhaul is the trucking industry's term for the return leg of a route — the haul back that a good dispatcher never lets run empty. The name plants the brand in real freight economics: the return trip should earn, not cost.
Modern.industrySummary: US retail returns reached roughly $890 billion in 2024 per NRF, and ecommerce return rates still run near double those of stores, so 2025-26 has become the era of returns triage: a majority of large retailers now charge for mail-back returns, keep-it refunds are algorithmically targeted, and returns fraud is estimated above $100 billion. Exchange-first software has become the standard playbook because saving 30-40% of refund revenue beats shaving pennies off label costs. Consolidation is underway — Happy Returns moved from PayPal to UPS, and box-free drop-off networks are now table stakes — pushing differentiation toward disposition intelligence and fraud screening.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Loop Returns (loopreturns.com) leads Shopify exchange-first returns; Happy Returns (happyreturns.com), now UPS-owned, owns the box-free drop-off network; Two Boxes (twoboxes.com) digitizes in-warehouse returns processing. Backhaul differentiates by unifying the shopper-facing exchange flow and the warehouse disposition decision in one rules engine, priced on revenue retained rather than per return.
Modern.positioningStatement: For DTC operators, Backhaul is the returns platform that measures itself in revenue saved, not returns processed.
Modern.positioningRationale: Every incumbent still reports volume metrics that make returns look like a cost center to minimize. Anchoring the entire product and pricing model to retained revenue reframes the category conversation and aligns Backhaul with the CFO, not just the ops manager.

targetAudience.primary: Heads of ecommerce operations and retention leads at DTC apparel, footwear, and home brands doing $5M-$150M online. They inherited a returns portal chosen by a predecessor, they present return-rate numbers to a CFO quarterly, and they are personally measured on contribution margin. They think in save-rates and refund-to-exchange ratios, not brand adjectives.

Modern.brandDescription: Saunders is a checkout optimization practice that ships every change as a controlled experiment and publishes every result — including the losers. Named for the inventor of self-service retail, Saunders treats the payment step as the most expensive real estate in commerce and refuses to redesign it on taste. Clients get a standing experiment program, a public ledger of what moved conversion and what didn't, and a team that argues from evidence or not at all.
Modern.brandNameRationale: Clarence Saunders founded Piggly Wiggly in 1916 and patented the self-service store, the single biggest checkout innovation in retail history. The name claims that lineage: every modern one-click flow descends from Saunders letting shoppers pick items themselves.
Modern.industrySummary: Baymard Research still pegs average cart abandonment near 70%, with checkout-usability failures alone worth an estimated $260B in recoverable orders across the US and EU. The 2025-26 twist is agentic commerce: accelerated wallets like Shop Pay and Link now anchor conversion benchmarks, while AI shopping agents begin completing purchases programmatically, forcing merchants to optimize for both the human thumb and the machine session. The one-click startup wave consolidated after Fast's 2022 collapse and Bolt's turbulence, shifting spend from magic-button vendors toward evidence-driven CRO programs.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Bolt (bolt.com) sells one-click checkout infrastructure; Fermat (fermatcommerce.com) spins up post-click buying experiences per ad; PrettyDamnQuick (prettydamnquick.com) runs checkout A/B testing for Shopify Plus. Saunders differs by operating as an open-ledger practice — methodology and anonymized results are public — rather than a software license, which converts skeptical CFOs the software vendors can't reach.
Modern.positioningStatement: Saunders is the checkout practice that would rather show you a losing test than sell you a winning story.
Modern.positioningRationale: CRO is a credibility-poor category full of cherry-picked case studies, so radical transparency is the scarcest asset a firm can own. Publishing the full ledger — wins, losses, and null results — makes every future claim cheaper to believe and turns the marketing function into the proof itself.

targetAudience.primary: VPs of ecommerce and growth leads at $20M-$500M retailers who have already bought two checkout tools that underdelivered. Psychographically they are burned skeptics: analytically fluent, allergic to vendor decks, and privately embarrassed by a checkout they know leaks. They will trade logo prestige for a partner who shows confidence intervals.

Modern.mission: To make checkout changes a matter of evidence.

Modern.manifesto: Every checkout is a hypothesis wearing a certainty costume. We take the costume off. We test the button, the field, the wallet order, the shipping reveal — and we write down what happened, even when what happened is nothing. Especially when it's nothing. The industry sells magic; we sell method. Saunders exists because the most profitable page on the internet deserves better than taste.

Modern.tagline: Own every mile of the message.
Modern.brandDescription: Between the buy button and the doorbell, most brands go silent and let a carrier template do the talking — Semaphore exists to end that. It is a post-purchase experience platform that replaces outsourced tracking emails and dead-end status pages with branded delivery narratives, accurate promise dates, and proactive delay messaging. Merchants on Semaphore routinely find the tracking page becomes the second-most-visited page on their store, and they learn to treat it accordingly.
Modern.scope: Branded order tracking, predictive delivery promises, delay and exception messaging, and post-purchase upsell modules for Shopify and composable stacks. Excludes last-mile carriage itself — Semaphore orchestrates the message layer over any carrier mix.
Modern.brandNameRationale: The semaphore was the 19th-century optical telegraph — towers relaying shipping and military news across France faster than any horse could carry it. It is the original technology for telling people where things are before they arrive, which is precisely the product.
Modern.industrySummary: 'Where is my order' contacts still consume 30-50% of ecommerce support volume, and in 2025-26 the delivery-promise engine has become a conversion lever: retailers showing confident, accurate dates at checkout convert measurably better than those showing carrier estimates. Carrier diversification after years of FedEx and UPS rate escalation means a typical mid-market brand now ships across four or more carriers, fragmenting tracking data precisely when shoppers expect Amazon-grade certainty. Incumbents are racing to bolt AI summarization onto tracking feeds, while merchants quietly discover the tracking page out-earns email for upsell impressions.
Modern.competitorLandscape: AfterShip (aftership.com) is the volume leader in multi-carrier tracking APIs; Narvar (narvar.com) owns the enterprise post-purchase suite; Wonderment (wonderment.com) serves Shopify brands with proactive shipping notifications. Semaphore differentiates on narrative control — a design-forward message layer with promise-date modeling — rather than raw carrier-integration counts.
Modern.positioningStatement: Semaphore is the platform that makes the wait between checkout and doorstep a branded experience instead of a carrier's afterthought.
Modern.positioningRationale: The post-purchase window is the only moment a customer checks their inbox hoping to hear from a brand, and most brands hand that attention to a UPS template. Claiming the message layer — not the logistics — lets Semaphore sit above carrier churn and sell to marketing and CX simultaneously.

Modern.brandDescription: Milkround is subscription management software modeled on the oldest recurring-commerce system that ever worked: the milkman's round. Pause, skip, swap, and 'not this week' are first-class actions on the customer's side of the gate, and cancellation is treated as a route change to be accommodated, not a failure to be dark-patterned away. Brands running on Milkround keep subscribers longer precisely because leaving was always easy.
Modern.brandNameRationale: The milk round — the daily doorstep delivery route of British dairies — ran on trust, flexibility, and a note left under the empty bottle: 'none today, extra Saturday.' It is the pre-digital proof that recurring revenue survives on manners, and the name imports that whole ethic.
Modern.industrySummary: Subscription commerce keeps growing through 2025-26, but the growth story has inverted from acquisition to retention: involuntary churn from failed payments accounts for roughly 40% of losses, and regulators have moved on the rest — the FTC's click-to-cancel push and state auto-renewal laws are forcing the industry to abandon cancellation mazes. Recharge dominates Shopify subscriptions while challengers compete on retention tooling, skip/swap UX, and AI churn prediction. The brands winning now publicize their easy cancel flows, because ease of exit has become a conversion argument.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Recharge (rechargepayments.com) is the category incumbent; Skio (skio.com) competes on modern passwordless subscriber UX; Smartrr (smartrr.com) sells retention-focused subscriber portals. Milkround differentiates by making generous-exit mechanics the brand promise itself, with churn analytics that treat a paused subscriber as a route change rather than a loss event.
Modern.positioningStatement: Milkround is the subscription platform for brands confident enough to make leaving easy.
Modern.positioningRationale: Regulation is about to outlaw what most retention tooling was built to do, which strands incumbents on the wrong side of the shift. Positioning generosity as strategy — backed by data showing easy-exit brands re-acquire lapsed subscribers cheaper — gives Milkround the regulatory tailwind as a brand story rather than a compliance scramble.

Many came up through customer support and still read cancellation surveys personally.

The platform is those ledgers, translated. The company's first design principle is still phrased the way her grandfather said it: 'the gate, not the padlock, keeps the customer.'

Modern.tagline: Eight cities. Every hour. On the map.
Modern.brandDescription: Density beats coverage — that is the entire strategy, and Crosstown wears it like a badge. Crosstown is a same-day delivery network for DTC brands that operates in exactly eight metros, publishes its coverage like a transit map down to the block, and promises windows it can actually hit because every route is crosstown, never cross-country. Brands route their urban orders through it and keep the national carriers for everywhere else.
Modern.scope: Same-day and next-day parcel delivery within eight US metros, with dark-store cross-docks, live route visibility, and a published on-time ledger per city. Deliberately excludes national linehaul, rural coverage, and freight.
Modern.brandNameRationale: Crosstown is transit vocabulary — the routes that cut across a city's grid rather than radiating from its center, prized by riders because they are short, frequent, and predictable. The name declares the operating doctrine: short urban legs, timetable honesty, no pretense of going everywhere.
Modern.industrySummary: The 2025-26 parcel market has fractured: years of UPS and FedEx general-rate increases and dimensional-weight tightening pushed shippers toward a booming regional-carrier layer, while consumer expectation in dense metros has compressed from two-day toward same-day. Venture-backed last-mile networks like Veho proved brands will re-platform urban volume for better economics, but overexpansion killed several players, making disciplined density the surviving strategy. Gig-economy cost inflation and city curb regulations increasingly favor operators with fixed routes and cross-dock infrastructure over pure crowdsourcing.
Modern.competitorLandscape: Veho (shipveho.com) runs next-day and same-day metro delivery for DTC brands; Roadie (roadie.com), UPS-owned, crowdsources same-day; Jitsu (gojitsu.com) operates AI-routed last-mile in major metros. Crosstown differentiates with a fixed eight-city footprint, published block-level coverage maps, and a public per-city on-time ledger no crowdsourced network can match.
Modern.positioningStatement: Crosstown is the same-day carrier that would rather own eight cities than touch forty.
Modern.positioningRationale: Every failed last-mile startup died of geographic ambition, so the refusal to expand is the credibility. A published transit-style map makes the constraint tangible and turns coverage honesty into the most differentiated marketing asset in a category built on asterisks.

targetAudience.primary: Logistics and fulfillment directors at DTC brands doing $30M+ with urban-skewed customer bases — beauty, fashion, wellness, small electronics. Demographically they cluster in the brand's own eight metros; professionally they carry carrier scorecards into quarterly reviews. They have been burned by a regional carrier's expansion promises before and now buy on published performance, not sales maps.

The result is a marketplace collectors cite the way they cite an auction catalogue.
Luxury.brandNameRationale: A catalogue raisonné is the definitive scholarly record of an artist's complete works — the document that settles attribution disputes and anchors value at auction. Taking the name commits the marketplace to that standard: the entry is the product as much as the object.
Luxury.industrySummary: The collectible design market matured sharply through 2025-26: 1stDibs' public filings show buyers consolidating toward trusted platforms, while a wave of misattributed 'in the style of' listings across mass marketplaces has made authentication the category's central anxiety. Gen Z and millennial buyers now drive the growth in 20th-century furniture, arriving via social discovery but converting only where provenance is documented. Auction houses have pushed downmarket with online-only design sales, squeezing undifferentiated dealers and rewarding platforms that can defend an attribution in writing.

Raisonné differentiates by publishing signed, referenced catalogue entries per object — scholarship as inventory — rather than seller-written descriptions behind a vetting badge.
Luxury.positioningStatement: Raisonné is the marketplace where the catalogue entry carries the same weight as the object.
Luxury.positioningRationale: In collectible design, the binding constraint on price is confidence, not desire — a documented attribution routinely doubles realized value. By making scholarship the product, Raisonné converts the category's deepest anxiety into its own moat, since entries compound into a citable reference archive competitors cannot retrofit.

Houses on Carnet sell to ninety markets without their brand ever meeting a customs surprise.
Luxury.scope: Duty and tax calculation, merchant-of-record services, localized checkout and payments, and white-glove cross-border fulfillment orchestration for luxury and premium brands. Excludes mass-market merchants by design — service density over merchant count.
Luxury.brandNameRationale: The ATA Carnet is the century-old 'passport for goods' — the customs document that lets valuables cross borders without duties or delay, used for couture shows and jewelry exhibitions to this day. The name places the brand inside the actual paperwork of the luxury trade.
Luxury.industrySummary: Cross-border DTC was upended in 2025 when the United States ended the $800 de minimis exemption — first for China-origin goods, then broadly — pushing duty calculation and customs strategy from back-office detail to boardroom topic. Global-e's growth showed luxury houses will outsource internationalization, while carriers and platforms scrambled to show landed-cost transparency at checkout as double-digit duty surprises became the top driver of cross-border cart abandonment. For 2026, winning vendors are those who can guarantee a delivered-duty-paid promise without degrading the brand experience that justifies luxury margins.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Global-e (global-e.com) is the enterprise cross-border leader; Zonos (zonos.com) specializes in landed-cost and duty APIs; Passport (passportglobal.com) runs international parcel and compliance for DTC brands. Carnet differentiates by refusing generality: luxury-only clientele, white-glove delivery orchestration, and after-sales service standards written into the SLA.
Luxury.positioningStatement: Carnet is the cross-border platform that treats customs as part of the client experience, not the fine print.
Luxury.positioningRationale: Luxury houses lose more brand equity to one customs-hostage delivery than to a season of discounting, yet generalist cross-border vendors optimize for volume economics that luxury does not need. A luxury-only mandate lets Carnet price on experience protection — the one metric maisons will always fund.

Luxury.brandDescription: Étrenne is a gifting house retained by families, firms, and founders to plan and execute an entire year of significant gifts in a single January sitting. Procurement-driven gifting has commoditized at exactly the moment relationship capital has become a stated board priority, and the luxury client's problem is not choice but cadence: remembering, deciding, and executing at standard, all year. Atelier sourcing and hand-finishing remain impossible to scale through marketplaces, which is precisely the moat for a retained service.
Luxury.competitorLandscape: Sendoso (sendoso.com) and Goody (ongoody.com) own volume corporate gifting; &Open (andopen.co) serves brand-led gifting for companies like Airbnb. Étrenne differentiates by abandoning the platform model entirely: an annual retainer, a January planning rite, and atelier-sourced execution — a private office, not a catalog.
Luxury.positioningStatement: Étrenne is the private gifting office that replaces a year of scrambling with one January afternoon.
Luxury.positioningRationale: At the top of the market, gifting fails on cadence and taste, not budget — the expensive-but-late gift is the category's signature disaster. Owning the calendar, not the catalog, moves Étrenne out of comparison with platforms and into the category of retained counsel, where pricing follows trust.

Into 2026, buyers are back but changed: they demand movement-level verification, service history, and water-resistance testing, not just a dial-side photo set, and platforms are competing on escrow, authentication depth, and watchmaker credentials rather than inventory breadth.

Poinçon differentiates by hallmarking: full disassembly and an in-house stamp on every piece, publishing bench documentation at a depth even CPO programs don't match.

Luxury.positioningRationale: Every trust signal in pre-owned watches — box, papers, dealer reputation — sits outside the case, while every expensive failure sits inside it. Sellers clear inventory at better recovery rates because informed bidders bid higher, and the data proves it quarterly.
Corporate.scope: Manifest-verified B2B auctions and negotiated sales of overstock, shelf-pulls, and customer returns across general merchandise, apparel, and consumer electronics. Excludes salvage-title vehicles, perishables, and unmanifested 'as-is' loads — the refusal is the product.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: A 'job lot' has been the trade's term for miscellaneous merchandise sold as one parcel since the 18th century, handled by the jobbers who moved goods between fortunes. The name takes the trade's own honest old word and attaches a modern instrument to it: the exchange, where standardized information makes prices real.
Corporate.industrySummary: The liquidation channel swelled through 2025-26 on the returns flood — nearly $890B in US returns annually feeds a reverse-supply chain that B-Stock and others have organized into a maturing secondary market, while bin stores and off-price retail boomed as inflation-weary consumers normalized buying liquidated goods. The trade's persistent defect is information asymmetry: unmanifested loads, padded manifests, and 'untested customer returns' language that shifts all risk to buyers and suppresses recovery rates for sellers. Retailers under margin pressure now treat recovery-rate improvement as a P&L program, rewarding channels that can prove data quality rather than just volume.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: B-Stock (bstock.com) runs the largest network of retailer liquidation marketplaces; Liquidation.com (liquidation.com) operates long-standing surplus auctions; Ghost (ghst.io) matches surplus inventory privately for brands. Joblot Exchange differentiates on manifest verification with published accuracy scores — an audited data layer where incumbents provide a listings layer.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Joblot Exchange is the liquidation marketplace where the manifest is underwritten, not just uploaded.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Recovery rates in liquidation are suppressed by risk discounts that exist only because information is unreliable, so verified data is literally worth margin to both sides. Auditing manifests against buyer receipts creates a trust flywheel — accuracy scores — that a volume-first incumbent cannot copy without re-underwriting its entire seller base.

targetAudience.primary: Two professional constituencies: inventory recovery managers at retailers and brands clearing overstock and returns, and the full-time resellers — bin-store operators, exporters, off-price buyers — who purchase by the pallet weekly. Both are spreadsheet-literate deal evaluators who have been burned by padded manifests and now discount everything. The buyer side skews owner-operator; the seller side reports recovery rates to a finance chain quarterly.

She built the verification protocol internally, watched recovery rates climb nine points, and left to build it as neutral infrastructure for the whole trade. The company's first hire was an auditor, not an engineer. Manifest accuracy scores have been published for every seller since the first quarter of operation.

Corporate.tagline: Paid by the beat we keep.
Corporate.brandDescription: Metronome Fulfillment is a third-party logistics operator built exclusively for subscription commerce, and it bills the way it performs: per cycle shipped complete and on time, not per pick, per touch, or per storage cubic foot. Kitting lines, custom inserts, and box-cycle changeovers are choreographed against each client's calendar, and when a cycle misses its window, the invoice says so before the client does. Metronome Fulfillment exists because recurring commerce lives or dies on rhythm, and rhythm deserved a pricing model.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: The metronome — perfected and patented by Johann Maelzel in 1815 — is the instrument that made tempo an objective, contractable standard for musicians. Adopting it names the company's entire premise: subscription logistics is tempo work, and the beat can be written into the contract.
Corporate.industrySummary: Subscription box commerce settled into disciplined maturity by 2025-26: the category's survivors run on retention economics where a late or wrong box measurably spikes churn, making fulfillment reliability a revenue variable rather than a cost line. The 3PL industry consolidated around technology platforms while per-touch pricing models kept punishing exactly what subscription brands need most — kitting complexity, inserts, and monthly changeovers billed as endless surcharges. Labor cost inflation and peak-cycle staffing remain the operational crux, favoring operators who can flatten demand spikes through cycle scheduling across a portfolio of clients.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: ShipMonk (shipmonk.com) is a technology-led 3PL with subscription capability; Fulfillrite (fulfillrite.com) specializes in subscription box and crowdfunding fulfillment; Fosdick Fulfillment (fosdickfulfillment.com) runs legacy direct-response and continuity programs. Metronome Fulfillment differentiates through cycle-based SLA pricing — compensation tied to on-time complete cycles — where competitors bill per activity regardless of outcome.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Metronome Fulfillment is the subscription 3PL whose invoice depends on the same thing the client's revenue does: the cycle shipping on time.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Per-activity billing misaligns 3PLs against subscription brands structurally — the warehouse profits from complexity while the brand profits from rhythm. Pricing on completed cycles aligns the P&Ls and converts the SLA from a negotiation artifact into the business model, a claim per-touch incumbents cannot make without rebuilding their economics.

targetAudience.primary: Operations directors and founders at subscription box companies shipping 10,000-500,000 boxes per cycle — meal-adjacent goods, beauty, hobby, pet, and curation brands. Professionally they are calendar people: their year is twelve (or twenty-six) hard deadlines, and they have all lived a cycle where the boxes went out four days late and the churn graph showed it. They negotiate 3PL contracts personally and read surcharge schedules like tax code.

Corporate.vision: A logistics industry where the invoice and the promise are the same document.

Corporate.manifesto: A subscription is a promise with a date on it. We think the company keeping that date should be paid for keeping it — not for every pick, every touch, every insert it can invoice along the way. So we put our fee where the client's revenue lives: the cycle, complete, on time. When we hit the beat, we bill in full. When we drop it, the invoice says so before the apology does. This is not generosity. It is the only honest way to run a warehouse that other people's promises depend on.

Corporate.tagline: Fraud stopped. Customers kept. Both numbers published.
Corporate.brandDescription: Floor Limit Systems is a fraud and chargeback prevention platform that reports its false-decline rate with the same prominence as its fraud-catch rate — because blocking a good customer is a loss the industry has agreed not to count. Its decisioning engine prices every order's risk against the lifetime value being risked, its chargeback team compiles evidence to card-network standards, and its quarterly client reports open with the revenue approved, not the fraud blocked. Floor Limit Systems sells protection that knows what it costs.
Corporate.scope: Order risk decisioning, chargeback representment, and friendly-fraud management for mid-market and enterprise merchants in retail, digital goods, and travel. Excludes crypto exchanges and adult verticals to keep underwriting posture clean.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: The floor limit was the card era's original risk rule: the transaction amount below which a merchant could accept a card without phoning the issuer for authorization, checking the printed warning bulletins for stolen numbers. The name honors the trade's oldest lesson — risk control has always been a threshold decision balancing loss against friction.
Corporate.industrySummary: Ecommerce fraud economics inverted in plain sight: industry studies consistently show false declines cost merchants several times more than fraud itself, with hundreds of billions in good orders refused annually while direct fraud losses run near $50B globally. Friendly fraud — customers disputing legitimate charges — now drives the majority of chargebacks, prompting Visa's CE3.0 compelling-evidence framework and a 2025-26 wave of first-party-misuse rule tightening across networks. AI-driven fraud rings industrialized attacks at the same moment AI decisioning matured, so vendor differentiation has shifted from detection accuracy claims to demonstrable approval-rate economics.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Signifyd (signifyd.com) and Riskified (riskified.com) lead guaranteed-fraud-protection decisioning for enterprise merchants; Chargeflow (chargeflow.io) automates chargeback recovery for SMB and mid-market. Floor Limit Systems differentiates by contractual transparency — false-decline rates published per client with insult-rate audits — where incumbents report primarily on fraud blocked.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Floor Limit Systems is the fraud platform that counts the customers it turns away.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Every vendor optimizes toward the metric it reports, and the industry reports fraud caught — so good customers quietly fund the difference. Publishing false-decline economics aligns the vendor with revenue rather than fear, and gives CFOs the number they never get: what protection actually costs in approved-order terms.

targetAudience.primary: Fraud and payments managers, VPs of risk, and ecommerce CFOs at merchants processing $50M-$2B annually. Job-title-led and metric-native: they own approval rates, chargeback ratios, and network compliance thresholds, and they sit in the crossfire between finance (wants approvals) and risk (wears the losses). Most have inherited a black-box vendor whose decline reasons they cannot explain to their own leadership.

Corporate.tagline: Marketplace growth, on an open book.
Corporate.brandDescription: Endcap Partners is a marketplace growth firm — Amazon, Walmart, TikTok Shop — compensated only on incremental profit and audited on it quarterly in an open-book review the client's finance team attends. Every dollar of retail media spend is defended line-by-line against incrementality tests; every fee traces to margin the client can verify in their own accounts. Endcap Partners grew on a heresy the agency world still resists: if the growth isn't provable, it isn't billable.
Corporate.brandNameRationale: The endcap is retail's most fought-over real estate — the aisle-end display where placement measurably moves volume, negotiated hard because its value can be counted. The name transplants that discipline to digital marketplaces: visibility is property, and property gets appraised.
Corporate.industrySummary: US retail media spend passed $60B annually and kept compounding into 2026, with Amazon capturing the bulk while Walmart Connect and TikTok Shop scaled fast — and with it grew the agency layer, validated publicly by Pattern's 2025 stock-market debut. The category's credibility problem compounded too: rising cost-per-clicks let agencies show revenue growth that was merely paid cannibalization of organic sales, and incrementality measurement became the sophisticated buyer's litmus test. Consolidation among full-service 'accelerators' has left a gap for firms that submit to financial audit rather than marketing-dashboard grading.
Corporate.competitorLandscape: Pattern (pattern.com) is the publicly listed ecommerce accelerator; Momentum Commerce (momentumcommerce.com) leads data-driven Amazon strategy for large brands; Envision Horizons (envisionhorizons.com) serves growth-stage marketplace brands. Endcap Partners differentiates on its compensation architecture — incremental-profit fees verified in quarterly open-book audits — versus retainer or revenue-share models graded on gross numbers.
Corporate.positioningStatement: Endcap Partners is the marketplace agency that invites the client's CFO to grade its homework.
Corporate.positioningRationale: Marketplace agencies are bought by marketing but increasingly killed by finance, because gross-revenue reporting hides cannibalized ad spend. Building the firm around incrementality audit makes finance the champion instead of the executioner, and repels exactly the clients — and competitors — who prefer flattering dashboards.

They are the people who noticed that last year's 40% Amazon growth somehow produced flat contribution margin. Skeptical by scar tissue, they read agency proposals with a calculator and have fired at least one vendor over attribution math.

Growth is what remains after you subtract what would have happened anyway — and if an agency won't run that subtraction, it is because the answer pays worse than the fiction. We invite the CFO to the review. We put our fees on the audited line. We cut spend that only buys back our clients' own organic sales, and we say so in writing. If that sounds unworkable, it is — for agencies that can't survive the math. We built the firm on it.

Creative.tagline: Step right up. Sell like you mean it.
Creative.brandDescription: Live shopping in America keeps failing for a reason nobody in the software business wants to hear: it's a performance problem, not a platform problem. Midway is a social commerce operations studio that trains brands in the barker's craft — hooks, bits, call-and-response, the turn — and then runs their TikTok Shop and live-selling operations end to end, from show calendars to inventory sync to creator casting. Midway treats a livestream like a carnival pitch with a cart button, because that is exactly what it is.
Creative.brandNameRationale: The midway is the carnival's central avenue, where pitchmen and talkers turned strolling crowds into paying ones using craft refined over a century of American fairs. The name claims that showmanship lineage as the missing discipline of social commerce.
Creative.industrySummary: TikTok Shop kept compounding US GMV through 2025 despite the divest-or-ban drama that ended in a US-controlled ownership deal, and live shopping — long dismissed as a China-only behavior — found its American foothold in collectibles, beauty, and fashion resale, with Whatnot's multi-billion GMV proving the entertainment-commerce model. The gap in the market is operational: brands know they need shoppable video and live programming but lack the performance skills and show-running infrastructure, and most agencies sell media buying rather than stagecraft. For 2026, retention economics favor brands that build recurring live audiences over those renting creator reach one post at a time.
Creative.competitorLandscape: CommentSold (commentsold.com) provides live-selling software for boutiques; Firework (firework.com) powers shoppable video for enterprise sites; TalkShopLive (talkshoplive.com) runs a live-shopping network with retail partners. All sell technology or airtime; Midway differentiates by selling the performance layer — barker training, show formats, and full show-running ops on top of whichever platform wins.
Creative.positioningStatement: Midway is the studio that treats live commerce as showbusiness with inventory.
Creative.positioningRationale: Software for live selling is commoditizing fast, but the ability to hold a crowd and turn it is scarce, teachable, and brand-defining — a human moat. Owning 'performance, not platform' lets Midway ride every app's rise without betting the firm on any of them.

targetAudience.primary: Social commerce leads and founders at consumer brands in beauty, collectibles, apparel, and food — plus the creators they cast. Psychographically they are the early-adopter showpeople of their companies: comfortable on camera or hungry to be, energized by live numbers climbing, impatient with brand teams that treat video like a print ad. Many grew up on QVC with a grandmother and won't admit how much they learned.

Creative.mission: To bring a century of showmanship to the shoppable screen.
Creative.vision: Every great brand running a live show its customers would watch even without the discount.
Creative.manifesto: The crowd hasn't changed. It never changes. It strolls, it skims, it dares you to be interesting — on a fairground avenue in 1935 or a For You page tonight. What changed is that brands forgot the craft: the hook thrown in three seconds, the bit that holds, the turn that sells without shame. We didn't invent any of this. The pitchmen did, the demonstrators did, the QVC hosts your grandmother trusted did. We just wrote it down, rehearsed it, and pointed it at a cart button. Step right up. The crowd can tell when you mean it.

Creative.tagline: Packaging with a second life printed on it.
Creative.brandDescription: Furoshiki is a packaging supplier for ecommerce brands that designs every mailer, box, and wrap around one creative constraint: the second use must be printed on the first. Boxes score-fold into hangers, drawer organizers, or picture frames; mailers carry stitch lines to become produce bags; tissue prints as gift wrap for the next occasion — instructions included, always. Furoshiki exists because the most honest sustainability claim a package can make is being worth keeping.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Furoshiki are the Japanese wrapping cloths used for centuries to carry and present goods, refolded and reused for a lifetime — a whole material culture built on the premise that the wrapping is never waste. The name imports that premise as a design brief for ecommerce packaging.
Creative.industrySummary: Packaging regulation got teeth in 2025-26: the EU's Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation entered application with recycled-content mandates and e-commerce void-space limits, several US states activated EPR fee schedules, and 'recyclable-ish' claims came under greenwashing enforcement. Meanwhile unboxing remains a marketing channel — brands still spend for the reveal moment — creating a genuine design brief: packaging that performs on camera, satisfies regulators, and doesn't feel like guilt in a box. Reuse-based models remain the category's hardest and least-solved frontier, mostly attempted through deposit-return schemes rather than design.
Creative.competitorLandscape: EcoEnclose (ecoenclose.com) leads research-grade sustainable packaging supply; noissue (noissue.co) owns accessible custom eco-packaging for small brands; Better Packaging Co (betterpackaging.com) built the compostable-mailer category. All optimize the disposal story; Furoshiki differentiates by designing for retention — the package's second use is the product spec, not an afterthought.
Creative.positioningStatement: Furoshiki is the packaging company that designs the afterlife first.
Creative.positioningRationale: Every competitor's pitch ends at the recycling bin, which consumers distrust and regulators increasingly audit — but an object kept is an impact claim no one can dispute and a brand impression that lasts months. Designing the second use into the first converts packaging spend from cost-plus-guilt into a keepsake media channel.

targetAudience.primary: Brand founders, creative directors, and packaging buyers at design-led DTC companies in beauty, apparel, home goods, and gifting — 5,000 to 500,000 shipments a year. Psychographically they are the people who keep beautiful boxes themselves and feel a twinge shipping bubble mailers. They approve packaging in the same meeting as brand campaigns, because to them it is one.

Creative.mission: To end single-use packaging by making the second use irresistible.
Creative.vision: A parcel economy where throwing away the box feels like throwing away part of the product.
coreValues: The afterlife is the design brief
Creative.manifesto: The wrapping was never supposed to be trash. For centuries a cloth carried the gift, then carried the groceries, then carried the next gift — and nobody wrote 'sustainable' on it, because keeping things was simply how things were kept. We make packaging the old way, with new dielines: every box knows what it becomes next, and says so, printed right there on the flap. Fold here. Keep this. We are done designing for the recycling bin and calling it responsibility. The bin is a confession. The shelf is the goal.

Creative.brandDescription: Edition of One is a print-on-demand network that treats the run-of-one as an art edition instead of a manufacturing compromise. Every piece ships numbered and dated, with the artist credited on a printed certificate, produced at a vetted print partner whose name appears in the colophon — and when a design is retired, it is retired forever, with the ledger public. Edition of One gives independent artists the economics of on-demand with the dignity of the print studio.
Creative.brandNameRationale: Edition numbering — 1/50, artist's proof, the crossed-out plate — is printmaking's centuries-old system for making multiples precious and provenance legible. Naming the company for the edition of one claims that tradition for on-demand production, where every print is its own complete edition.
Creative.industrySummary: Print-on-demand consolidated dramatically with the Printful-Printify merger announced in late 2024, concentrating mass POD into a scale-and-price game just as AI image generators flooded marketplaces with low-effort designs — Etsy and Amazon Merch both tightened policies against AI slop through 2025. The resulting trust collapse created a countermarket: buyers and legitimate artists seeking provenance, quality control, and scarcity signals that mass POD structurally cannot offer. Premium POD in 2026 competes on print partner quality, artist verification, and story — the exact attributes commodity platforms strip out.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Printful (printful.com) and Printify (printify.com), now merging, dominate commodity POD; Gelato (gelato.com) runs the global local-production network. All compete on catalog breadth and unit cost; Edition of One differentiates with edition discipline — numbering, certificates, named print partners, and permanent retirement — selling scarcity logic in an infinite-supply category.
Creative.positioningStatement: Edition of One is the print-on-demand network where infinite supply ends and editions begin.
Creative.positioningRationale: Mass POD's race to zero has made 'print-on-demand' a synonym for disposable, which punishes exactly the artists with real audiences and real standards. Importing printmaking's edition conventions rebuilds the scarcity and provenance that justify honest prices — a position the merged giants cannot copy without contradicting their own economics.

targetAudience.primary: Working illustrators, tattoo artists, muralists, and graphic artists with engaged followings of 5,000-500,000 — people who sell out drops but refuse to babysit inventory. Psychographically they are craft-proud and platform-burned: they've watched their work ripped by AI stores, taken 70-cent margins from commodity POD, and quietly stopped promoting their own shops out of embarrassment. They talk about paper stock the way chefs talk about produce.

Creative.mission: To give every on-demand print the provenance of the studio it came from.
Creative.vision: An internet where owning a print by a living artist means something again.
coreValues: Print partners are named, never hidden

Creative.manifesto: A print used to be a promise: this many, no more, signed by the hand that made it. Then infinite supply arrived and called itself democratization while paying artists in cents. We refuse the cheapness, not the technology. Print one at a time — but number it, date it, name the press, credit the artist, and when it's done, let it be done. Scarcity was never about the count. It was about the word being kept. Edition of One keeps the word.
Creative.scope: On-demand production and fulfillment of numbered art prints, apparel, and objects through a vetted press network, with artist verification, certificates, and a public retirement ledger. No AI-generated catalogs, no unlicensed designs, no anonymous production.

Creative.tagline: The fitting comes before the fabric.
Creative.brandDescription: Toile is fit technology named for the muslin test garment every atelier sews before cutting real cloth, and it makes the same promise to online shoppers: the fitting happens before the purchase. A two-minute guided capture builds a private body profile, and from then on every product page answers the only question that matters — how this garment falls on this body — with a visual drape preview instead of a size chart. Brands running Toile watch bracketing collapse because shoppers stop ordering three sizes to conduct the fitting at home.
Creative.brandNameRationale: The toile is couture's rehearsal garment — the cheap cloth version where fit is perfected before scissors touch the silk. The name honors the atelier truth the industry forgot when it moved online: fitting is a step, not a gamble, and it belongs before the commitment.
Creative.industrySummary: Fit remains apparel ecommerce's most expensive unsolved problem into 2026: size-related issues drive the majority of apparel returns, and bracketing — deliberately ordering multiple sizes — became so normalized that retailers began charging for returns partly to tax it. The fit-tech field split between size-recommendation engines trained on purchase data and computer-vision body measurement, while 2025's generative-AI leap made photoreal virtual try-on genuinely plausible for the first time — and simultaneously raised shopper privacy sensitivity about body data. Brands now evaluate fit tools on return-rate deltas and data governance together, not demo sizzle.
Creative.competitorLandscape: True Fit (truefit.com) runs the largest fit-data network across retailers; Fit Analytics (fitanalytics.com), Snap-owned, leads size recommendation for global brands; Bold Metrics (boldmetrics.com) builds digital-twin body models for apparel. All lead with recommendation percentages; Toile differentiates with the visual drape preview — showing fall and fit on the shopper's own proportions — plus body data that never leaves the shopper's control.
Creative.positioningStatement: Toile is the fit platform that replaces the size chart with a fitting.
Creative.positioningRationale: Size charts ask shoppers to do arithmetic about their own bodies, and recommendation engines ask them to trust a percentage — neither shows the garment falling on them, which is what a fitting is. Owning the drape preview positions Toile where the category is heading while its privacy-first architecture answers the objection that will define it.

targetAudience.primary: Shoppers aged 25-55 whose bodies don't match the fit model — which is to say, nearly everyone: petite and tall ranges, between-sizes, post-partum, athletic builds. Psychographically they are the burned-by-bracketing majority who keep a return pile by the door and a mental list of brands whose mediums lie. On the buying side: ecommerce directors at apparel brands with return rates above 30% who have already tried a quiz widget and can quote its non-impact.

Creative.mission: To put the fitting back before the purchase, where the atelier always kept it.
Creative.vision: Apparel commerce where the size chart is a museum piece.
coreValues: Show the drape, don't state the odds

Returns are a design failure, not a shopper failure
Creative.story: Toile's founding team pairs a former Savile Row cutter with a computer-vision researcher who met, improbably, at a conference panel on returns. The cutter said something that reorganized the engineer's roadmap: 'You're all building better guessing. A fitting is not a guess — it's a rehearsal.' They spent eighteen months teaching software what a drape rehearsal requires — cloth behavior, posture, proportion — and named the company for the muslin that has rehearsed every great garment for two centuries. The first pilot brand cut size-related returns by a third; its founder mailed them an actual toile, signed.

Creative.tagline: Ask for Ruth. She remembers you.
Creative.brandDescription: Switchboard is an ecommerce customer-service studio that staffs brands the way a 1920s telephone exchange staffed a town: named operators, known voices, and no tickets — conversations. Every customer who writes twice gets the same operator twice; every operator signs their name, keeps their own follower base of regulars, and holds real authority to refund, replace, and decide. Switchboard sells the one thing AI made scarce overnight: being known by the person who answers.
Creative.brandNameRationale: The switchboard operator — the 'hello girl' of the early telephone exchange — was the original customer-experience professional: she knew every subscriber by name, routed by memory, and held the town's trust through her headset. The name revives that standard as a deliberate counterposition in the automation era.
Creative.industrySummary: AI agents crossed the competence line in 2025 — platforms like Sierra and Decagon resolve the majority of tier-1 ecommerce contacts, Gorgias and Zendesk shipped native AI resolution, and the offshore BPO layer is being squeezed from both ends. The strategic consequence is bifurcation: routine support races to zero cost while a premium tier emerges where human attention itself is the product, mirroring what happened to retail banking tellers and hotel concierges. Into 2026, brands with high LTV and community-driven growth are re-hiring humanity deliberately — and discovering that named, continuous, empowered agents measurably lift repeat purchase where anonymous ticket queues never did.
Creative.competitorLandscape: Influx (influx.com) provides flexible outsourced ecommerce support teams; TalentPop (talentpop.com) staffs dedicated agents for DTC brands; Gorgias (gorgias.com) is the dominant helpdesk software layer with AI resolution. The outsourcers sell coverage and the software sells deflection; Switchboard differentiates by selling continuity — named operators with regulars, authority, and tenure — as a retention product priced against LTV, not per ticket.
Creative.positioningStatement: Switchboard is the support studio for brands that want customers greeted by name in an economy of deflection.
Creative.positioningRationale: As AI makes competent-but-anonymous service free, its value falls to zero and the differentiated asset becomes memory — the operator who knows the customer's dog, order history, and last complaint. Selling continuity as a retention investment moves Switchboard out of the cost-center conversation entirely, which is the only conversation the ticket-priced incumbents can have.

targetAudience.primary: Founders and heads of CX at high-LTV, community-powered brands — specialty hobby, premium pet, collectibles, craft supplies, luxury consumables — where customers write in five times a year and know the brand's staff by name already. Psychographically they are hospitality people trapped in software people's tooling: they answer DMs personally at midnight, they can name their hundred best customers, and they view every automated 'We've received your request!' email as a small betrayal.

Creative.mission: To keep human memory in commerce — one named operator at a time.
Creative.vision: A market where 'who answers your email' is a brand differentiator listed on the homepage.
coreValues: Warmth with competence, never instead of it
Creative.manifesto: Somewhere along the way, service became deflection and a person became a ticket. We remember it differently. We remember when the operator knew your name before you said it, because knowing was the job. So we staff the old way: real names, real memory, real authority to fix the thing without asking permission. The machines can fetch the tracking number — good, let them. But the conversation belongs to a human who will still be here when you write back in March. Ask for Ruth. She remembers you. That sentence is our entire business plan.
